problem: End-to-end trained navigation agents are black boxes; existing interpretability tools for image classifiers ignore the rich simulator metadata, and prior embodied-AI probing does not identify which individual hidden units encode a concept.
motivation: Interpretability matters before deploying embodied agents on real robots. Simulators give free ground-truth metadata (target visibility, reachability, visit history), so one can probe recurrent hidden states for human-interpretable concepts and locate the units that carry them.
key_idea: Train gradient-boosted trees to predict simulator metadata concepts from an agent's GRU hidden state, use SHAP to find the top-k relevant units per concept, and verify their causal role by ablating those units.
insight: Concepts are stored sparsely: about 50/512 units for ObjectNav target info and 5/512 for PointNav, and SHAP values drop sharply after a few units. Ablating 10 target units cuts ObjectNav SPL far more than removing 50 random units, so the units are causally important. Random baselines show that reachability in PointNav comes largely from GPS input and ImageNet-pretrained ResNet features rather than from training. PointNav agents rely on GPS and less on vision.
method: Metadata extraction: from AI2-THOR, extract target distance/orientation, target visibility and pixel area, agent distance/orientation from spawn, reachability of grid points at radii 2/4/6 x grid size in 30° steps, and visited location/rotation/horizon history.

Probing agents: ResNet18 (frozen) or SimpleConv encoder plus goal embedding feed a GRU with 512 units; agents are trained with AllenAct for 300M steps, and untrained random baselines are used for comparison.

Human trajectories: all agents are forced to follow the same human-driven trajectories (59 train and 42 val episodes, about 480 steps each) with deliberate collisions and revisits, giving 28k train and 20k val samples.

GBT concept prediction: one xgboost tree (depth 10) per concept maps GRU activations to metadata, using logistic loss for binary concepts and MSE for continuous ones, and is scored by correlation or ROC-AUC on validation scenes.
SHAP unit attribution: TreeSHAP gives exact Shapley values per unit, aggregated as mean |SHAP| over the validation set to rank units and give direction via beeswarm plots.
Unit ablation: set the top-k relevant units to their training-mean activation and measure SPL, success and episode length against random-unit ablation.

setting.backbone: ResNet18 (frozen, ImageNet) + GRU, or 5-layer SimpleConv + GRU (trained with RL in AllenAct); GBT + SHAP as probe
setting.training_data: RL in iTHOR rooms for 300M steps (AllenAct default hyperparameters); probes trained on 28k samples from human trajectories
setting.observation: egocentric RGB; PointNav also gets GPS+compass target distance and orientation
setting.privileged: simulator metadata used only for probing and analysis, not by the agent

numbers_note: No standard benchmark results. Agent performance (at ~50M steps): ObjectNav ResNet18 success 0.458 / SPL 0.23, SimpleConv 0.124 / 0.056; PointNav ResNet18 0.925 / 0.755, SimpleConv 0.878 / 0.712, on the authors' own iTHOR split, not a canonical benchmark.
results: The trained ResNet ObjectNav agent encodes reachability (corr 0.45, ROC-AUC 0.75 for the front), target information and visit history better than the random and SimpleConv baselines. Ablating 10 target units sharply lowers SPL, while removing random units has little effect. In PointNav, units for agent distance overlap with target-distance units, and removing them drives success to almost zero.
limitations: Units are analysed individually, so concepts distributed across multiple units are not captured; the constant units found for R_a are only explained via combination with target units.
Only a fixed set of hand-chosen concepts, simple GRU navigation agents and a single simulator (AI2-THOR) are studied; the irrelevant-unit ablation shows unexplored concepts remain.
SHAP relevance is correlational and needs ablation to show causality.
compares_to: Linear probing of hidden states (Weihs et al.)
Fixed point analysis of RNN units (Ye et al.)
